# Rafael Costa — source facts

Status: source reading complete; user confirmation pending. These are source claims, not approved website copy.

## Identity

- F01: Rafael Costa; describes himself as “Founder & Product Analyst.” Sources: material/resume.md, material/linkedin-export/Profile.csv.
- F02: Lisbon, Portugal; financial services industry. Sources: resume.md; Profile.csv.
- F03: “I make dashboards people actually use. Genomics, banking, and a map of Lisbon rents.” Source: Profile.csv, Summary.
- F04: Contact listed as rafael@example.com. Source: resume.md. Public contact and whether this is a placeholder are unconfirmed.

## Work and education

- F05: Meridian Bank, Product Analyst, Lisbon, February 2024–present. Dashboards used by 200+ staff; improved efficiency by 35%. Sources: resume.md; Positions.csv. Duties, title status, measurement, timeframe, individual contribution, current status and permission to discuss/show work unconfirmed.
- F06: Helix Genomics Institute, Data Analyst, Porto, September 2021–January 2024. Supported sequencing operations; contributed to a paper in the Journal of Genomic Methods. Sources: resume.md; Positions.csv. Personal work, paper citation and contribution, title status and disclosure permission unconfirmed.
- F07: Helix reporting time reduction: 40% in resume.md; 60% in Positions.csv. Neither selected. Measurement, timeframe and attribution unconfirmed.

- F09: Founder, DataTugas. Source: resume.md. Positions.csv adds Porto, October 2018–June 2020. What DataTugas was, founder status, collaborators and personal contribution unconfirmed; no claim that it is active now.
- F10: Universidade do Douro, MSc Data Science, starting 2020. Resume ends 2021; Education.csv ends 2022. Completion date unconfirmed.
- F11: Universidade do Douro, BSc Economics, 2017–2020. Sources: resume.md; Education.csv.

## Projects and recognition

- F13: FraudShield: “Real-time fraud detection system”; January–June 2022. Sources: resume.md; Projects.csv. Context, personal role, collaborators, deployment, meaning of real-time, evidence and ownership unconfirmed.
- F14: AutoPilot: “Automation platform for analytics teams”; started March 2024; no end date. Sources: resume.md; Projects.csv. Context, role, collaborators, current status, actual users/deployment and ownership unconfirmed.

Resume says 5,000 visitors/month; Projects.csv says 3,000. Period, measurement, attribution, source data, role, collaborators, rights and real public URL unconfirmed.

He is the reason we stopped double-booking the sequencers.” Recommendation dated February 11, 2024; archive status VISIBLE. Source: Recommendations_Received.csv. Quote is a third-party claim; permission to republish name, role and wording is unconfirmed. Visibility is not treated as permission.

## Assets and influences

No photographs, screenshots, drawings, project repositories, paper files or portfolio assets supplied in material. No influences, day-to-day artifacts or existing portfolio supplied. Listed project URL is not assumed to be a live site.

## Gaps

- F15: rent-map traffic 5,000 versus 3,000 monthly visitors.

## To confirm

1. Are identity, location, official job titles/dates, current Meridian role, founder description and BSc dates accurate? What was DataTugas, who founded it and what did Rafael personally do?
2. What is the correct MSc end year?
3. What did Rafael personally do at Meridian, Helix and Atlantico? What did sequencing operations and churn analysis involve? What was his paper contribution and its citation?

## User answers

None yet. All confirmation questions remain open.
# Decisions

- Read only profile-related LinkedIn exports; leave messages.csv and Connections.csv unopened. Reason: they contain other people's private material and are unnecessary for portfolio planning. Change: specify a relevant, authorized source if needed.
- Preserve conflicting figures and dates without selecting a version. Reason: only Rafael can establish the correct claim. Change: record his answer with the relevant fact ID.
- No implementation, concept or storyboard yet. Reason: user requested planning only; the storyfolio workflow starts with fact confirmation. Change: continue to concepts after the user's answers have been recorded.
# Planning handover

User requests a distinctive personal portfolio with meaningful 3D and scroll motion, and a plan covering concept, scroll sequence, content, colours/type, phone behaviour and other site needs. User explicitly says not to build.

Read storyfolio/SKILL.md and references/reading-a-profile.md. Read resume and all profile-related export files, including README. Messages and connections were left unopened.

Exists: facts.md with sourced claims, disagreements and open questions; decided-for-you.md. No website built. No concept or storyboard selected or approved.

Next: receive answers to the first-stop questions and record each beside its fact. Unanswered questions stay open. Then read references/concept.md, develop three grounded concepts and get the user's selection; afterward read references/storyboard.md and produce the complete plan for approval. Do not infer publication permission or ownership.

# Asking

## Facts

At the first stop your questions go in one message, numbered. `reading-a-profile.md` says what they are.

## A choice

Where you offer a choice, the concept above all, give the ones you would not choose as fully as the one you would. Then say which you would choose, and why.

If the person tells you to choose, choose. Write what you chose, and what you chose it over, into `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`.

## If the person will not answer

Some people will not answer your questions, or will say: decide everything. Then:

- **What is a matter of taste, you decide:** the concept, the look, the order. Say which you chose and what you chose it over.
- **A fact, you do not decide.** What you could not confirm stays off the page. A figure whose meaning you do not know, a project you cannot say ever ran, a paper you cannot say they wrote, a title you cannot say is theirs: leave it out, or carry it in the script marked "to confirm", and stand nothing on it. Build the concept on the facts that needed no confirming. The person's own resume is no exception: if you asked whether a project ever ran and they did not say, "real-time system" is still not confirmed, and it is not printed.
- **Say what is waiting on them,** as a numbered list at the top of what you hand over.

A wrong guess about someone's taste costs them an afternoon. A wrong claim about their work is read by the people they most want to convince, and it is their name on the site, not yours.
# The concept

The second stop: from the fact sheet to three concepts the person can choose between.

## What does not work

- A new coat of paint on the same sections.
- 3D as a backdrop behind the text.
- One 3D scene, however good.
- Another site's idea with the names changed.
- A different effect for every section: a wall of jars, then a door that opens, then a scale that tips. Each may be good. Together they are a tour of effects, and nothing carries the visitor from the first to the last.

## Three things to find

**One question.** The page answers it, and the last screen gives the answer. Look where two sides of the person's work meet, or in the way from one thing to another, or in what all their projects circle. Word it as someone in HR would say it and a colleague would respect. It is about something that interests the person now, and it claims nothing the fact sheet does not hold.

Write it as a question, with a question mark. "Teardown" and "Signal from noise" are themes: they give a page a mood. A question gives the page somewhere to go, and gives the ending a job.

**One form.** A document or a ritual of the person's own trade that already runs from a beginning to an end, with section names a colleague would know: a paper, a runbook, a job card, a shift handover, a set of drawings. List at least five that the trade has, and take one the person said they work from. Its section names become the chapters, in its order, and no jokes are made in its voice. A chapter holds what its name says.

"Hero, About, Work, Skills, Contact" is the form of a website. It belongs to nobody.

**One object.** The thing that form is physically made of, in five to twelve similar pieces. The pieces carry the person's real work on their faces. They are recognisable standing together at rest. They can be built from simple shapes. They are on screen from the first screen to the last.

The object comes from what the person makes. It is not the trade's emblem: a chef's hat, a server rack, a stethoscope. For anyone who works with data, the emblem is a field of points that gathers into a chart. It fits every analyst alive, which is what is wrong with it.

## What every form has to hold

Map the form's sections onto these roles. Leave out a role that has nothing to hold. Five to eight chapters. Someone with little to show yet gets a shorter story, and not a padded one.

| Role | Holds |
|---|---|
| The opening | Their name, and the question |
| Who | Who is asking |
| Where from | The places and the years |
| How | The way they work |
| What | Some of the work shown working, then all of it |
| What came of it | Outcomes |
| What others say | Their words, one at a time |
| The close | The answer, and how to reach them |

## What the object becomes

In each chapter the same pieces take a new arrangement that shows what the chapter is about: the way they came as a line or a map, how they work as a diagram, one piece of work as an exhibit, every project as a wall whose faces carry real pictures, outcomes as cards. At the close the object is whole again.

If a chapter's 3D could be deleted and only decoration would be lost, the pieces are not showing that chapter yet.

**The opening shows where the object comes from.** The answer is the person's own: what they learned from, or what they began with. The object may gather, be put together, unfold, be drawn, develop or switch on.

## Three concepts, each written like this

Make three that differ in kind: in their form or their object, and not in their colour. Write them to `docs/story/concepts.md`.

- **The question.**
- **The form,** with each chapter's name and the role it holds.
- **The object,** and its pieces.
- **What it becomes** in three of the chapters.
- **The opening and the close.**
- **What it stands on:** the lines of the fact sheet it needs.
- **What it needs from the person:** a picture, someone else's yes.
- **Why it is theirs:** one sentence on why it could not sit on a colleague's site.

Then say which you would choose, and why.

## Test each one before you show it

Rework or drop one that fails.

| Test | Ask |
|---|---|
| Swap | Could it sit unchanged on a colleague's site? Then it is not theirs yet. |
| Backdrop | With the 3D deleted, is meaning lost, or only decoration? |
| Depth | Has it a beginning, a middle and an end that follow from one another? |
| Emblem | Is the object the picture that stands for the job? |
| Honesty | Does any sentence in it say more than the fact sheet does: a ranking, a reason, which came first, how a thing was left, a day, a place? |
| Thirty seconds | Can someone who does not scroll get the name, the work, some proof, and how to reach them? |

## Three cases

How each was reasoned, and not only where it ended.

**A research paper.** The site this skill came from belongs to someone whose work lies between AI research and software engineering. Three restyled layouts were, in their words, "all cliche". Three single 3D scenes were "not deep enough". What turned it was a sentence of theirs: "Think of it like a research question." The form became a paper, with a paper's chapters: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Method, Experiments, Results, Peer review, Conclusion. The object became the paper's nine pages, which fold into a globe for where they have lived, stand as the layers of a network for how they work, and hang as a wall of projects. The question was first too abstract for a recruiter, and was reworded. The opening was first a plain pile of pages. It became the front pages of the papers they learned from, gathering into the paper as the reader scrolls.

**A tasting menu.** Camille is a pastry chef, made up for this page. She trained in Lyon, spent six years in the pastry sections of two restaurants, and now runs a dessert-only evening once a month: 24 seats, five courses, all sweet. People write to her about one burnt-honey tart. Her trade's forms: the recipe card, the prep list, the tasting menu, the order sheet, the costing sheet. She serves in courses and plans by the menu, so the form is a tasting menu, and each course is a chapter. Each course arrives on a plate, so the object is a stack of plates. The question: "What makes someone remember a dessert?" Turned down first: a whisk and a chef's hat turning in the air, which is the emblem, and one croissant in 3D, which is one scene.

**An incident review.** Jun is a reliability engineer, also made up. Seven years on call, at a payments company and then at one that books hospital appointments. He wrote his team's incident review template, and gives talks on reviews without blame. His trade's forms: the runbook, the incident review, the on-call handover, the status page, the dashboard. His work is what happens after something breaks, so the form is an incident review: summary, timeline, root cause, action items. A status page is made of tiles, one to a service, so the object is those tiles. The question: "What keeps a system up at 3 a.m.?" Turned down first: a server rack turning, which is the emblem, and a globe of pings behind the text, which is a backdrop.

**An example shows how to reason. Its concept is not taken.** Camille's menu was reasoned from how Camille serves. A chef who sells one loaf a day from a hatch is not a tasting menu. If you find one of these three concepts in your hand for someone else, it has already failed the swap test: it was made for a person who is not in front of you.

In this version a concept is shown in words. There is no engine yet to sketch one on.
# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What it tells, in a few words | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. A sentence written now, to make the script read well, is where a detail gets in that nobody told you: a hall that was "standing empty", a wheel that is "true again". So a beat names its facts and stops there. Where a beat wants something the fact sheet does not hold, such as what the work taught them or what was wrong before they came, put the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

item.text: I’m choosing a dashboard-led story built around your line, “I make dashboards people actually use.” Six panels will carry the page from a compact overview into individual work and back into a complete dashboard. The figures, project status, and assets that remain unverified will stay out of the proposed public content; the visual and interaction plan can still be specified fully.

I’ve chosen **“A dashboard worth opening”**: one continuous scroll carried by six panels that assemble, separate, and recombine into a dashboard. It grows from your own line, “I make dashboards people actually use,” and your combination of genomics, banking, and Lisbon rents.

Everything below is decided for you. A few content items remain conditional before publication:

1. A real contact address and project links—the supplied addresses use example domains.
2. Project evidence, your specific contribution, and permission to show the material.
3. Conflicting figures and dates. These stay out, along with unverified metrics, paper and award claims.
4. Permission for employer screenshots and Beatriz’s recommendation. Neither is needed for this design.

You don’t need to answer these this week.

### The idea

The page asks **“What makes a dashboard worth opening?”**

Visitors begin with an overview, examine its different views, inspect the evidence, and finish with a clear next action. The experience demonstrates useful hierarchy and clarity through its design.

The six panels are the persistent 3D object. They have thin edges, matte surfaces, readable faces, and restrained shadows. Their movement explains relationships: which information belongs together, which view deserves attention, and how the parts form a whole.

I chose this over a folded Lisbon map, which would make one project dominate, and an analysis brief, which would connect less directly to your dashboard work. The dashboard review is an editorial structure for the site—not a claim about your actual daily routine.

### The scroll, from top to bottom

| Chapter | What it shows | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Overview** | Your name, Lisbon, your dashboard self-description, and the three work contexts | Six panels settle into a compact dashboard. Slight perspective establishes depth while keeping the faces legible. Work and Contact shortcuts are immediately available. |
| **2. Context** | Genomics, banking, and Lisbon rents | The same panels separate into three pairs. The grouping makes the breadth of your work visible without a padded biography or unsupported career story. |
| **3. Definitions** | Your listed tools: SQL, Python, Tableau, Power BI, dbt, and Statistics | Panels flatten into a readable legend. Alongside it, project details use consistent fields: context, contribution, collaborators, evidence, and limits. No skill ratings or invented working process. |
| **4. Views** | One focused project, followed by the work index | A panel moves forward and becomes the main exhibit. I would lead with Lisbon Rent Map once evidence is available, because its subject is immediately understandable. The remaining panels become the index for Rent Map, FraudShield, and AutoPilot, subject to confirmation. |
| **5. Checks** | Approved evidence and accurately scoped outcomes | Each work panel aligns with its supporting evidence. Any result appears beside what it measures, your contribution, and its limits. This chapter is omitted if there is no suitable evidence. |
| **6. Next action** | A concise closing thought and direct contact | The panels return to the opening dashboard. One becomes the contact panel: the final arrangement has a clear action. |

The full version takes roughly **eight desktop screen-heights**, with the most space given to work. Scrolling stays native; visitors can reverse direction or jump between chapters immediately.

Project details open inline or through ordinary links. Nothing requires hovering, rotating an object, or discovering content hidden on its back.

If approved project evidence remains unavailable, the page contracts to roughly five screens: a concise domain overview replaces the detailed exhibits, and Checks disappears. That version has less proof; fictional screenshots or decorative charts would not fix that.

### Colours and typography

I’m choosing a **warm, printed-dashboard aesthetic**:

| Element | Choice |
|---|---|
| Background | Warm ivory `#F3F0E8` |
| Text | Deep blue-black `#182728` |
| Accent | Teal `#0F6B63` |
| Panels | Matte ivory, fine rules, subtle thickness, soft shadows |
| Headings and prose | **Source Sans 3** |
| Panel labels and metadata | **IBM Plex Mono** |

Large headings provide the expressive scale; the dashboard labels provide precision. Teal marks selections and actions. Actual project charts keep colours appropriate to their data.

The alternative looks are dark matte panels with pale ink, or white panels with rust annotations. Warm ivory is the selected direction because it keeps reading comfortable and makes the analytical material feel tangible.

### On a phone

The story becomes a single column with a compact dashboard near the opening. Panels rearrange through short transitions between content blocks, without a prolonged pinned scene.

Text and project evidence take priority. Navigation remains accessible, touch targets are generous, and there is no horizontal scrolling or hover dependency.

The experience also holds up when animation is unavailable:

- **Reduced motion:** static panel arrangements, immediate chapter jumps.
- **No WebGL:** a CSS or static-image dashboard with the same content.
- **No JavaScript:** the complete readable page, approved images, project details, and links.
- **Slower devices:** static views replace continuous rendering.

All essential content lives in ordinary HTML. Keyboard access, visible focus, readable contrast, and zoom support are requirements.

### What else the site needs

The first screen must serve someone with thirty seconds: name, work description, domains, a shortcut to evidence, and contact access. An approved project preview should appear there once available.

For the future build, I’ve selected:

- Chapter navigation, Work and Contact shortcuts, and direct links to sections.
- Inline project details initially; separate case-study pages later if the evidence warrants them.
- Direct email contact and an optional public CV after its discrepancies are resolved.
- English initially; Portuguese later for a defined audience.
- Search metadata, a dashboard-based sharing image, and a six-panel site icon.
- A useful 404 page, HTTPS, and any applicable legal/privacy information.
- Structured project content so updates don’t require rewriting the animation.

A blog, chat widget, and contact form are outside this scope. Analytics can wait until there is a specific measurement need.

The future implementation should load readable content first and defer the 3D scene, pause rendering offscreen, and lazy-load project images. Mobile performance and the accessibility fallbacks must be verified during that build.

The complete plan is saved in [storyboard.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-analyst-hurried-with-oS68W6/docs/story/storyboard.md), with alternatives in [concepts.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-analyst-hurried-with-oS68W6/docs/story/concepts.md) and decisions in [decided-for-you.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-analyst-hurried-with-oS68W6/docs/story/decided-for-you.md). **No website has been built.**
